objections.question: Does the business work financially?
objections.objection: Base case loses ₹138 per kit once founder time is paid, and peak cash of about ₹7.7 lakh is about 2.6 times the ₹3 lakh budget.

objections.question: What could make this fail?
objections.objection: A termiticide sealant is likely a regulated pesticide product; registration time and cost could exceed the ₹2.5 lakh assumed and push first revenue well past 233 days. This is reasoning, not a verified rule.

objections.question: Does something similar already exist?
objections.objection: Board makers already tell carpenters to treat cut edges with borate, and Greenply moves treatment into the board core to avoid the cut-edge problem. Leaders are solving it at the board level.

objections.question: Which assumption is least reliable?
objections.objection: That carpenters will brush every edge and homeowners will check with a torch. Both add effort for people who did not ask for it.

objections.question: Would anyone pay for this?
objections.objection: No buyer has confirmed the problem or a price; demand is level 1.

critique:cpt_5af7828f45.strongest_point: It targets the real weak point, cut edges, which board makers themselves acknowledge.
critique:cpt_5af7828f45.simpler_alternative: Skip the product. Offer the tracer idea to a board maker as a licensed add-on to their own edge-treatment advice, or publish a free edge-treatment checklist that names an existing borate product.

objections.question: Does the business work financially?
objections.objection: Each set loses money before fixed costs once the 25% dealer margin, ₹267 acquisition per set and ₹150 courier are paid.

objections.question: What could make this fail?
objections.objection: Termite shields mainly make infestations visible; they do not prevent them. Selling this as protection would overstate it.

objections.question: What could make this fail?
objections.objection: Ant caps fail when timber fixtures bridge them. Carpenters routinely add trims and fillers that would close the gap.

objections.question: Can it be manufactured or delivered?
objections.objection: Tall wardrobes held 30 mm off the wall on brackets raise tipping and anchor pull-out risks; this needs load testing and a structural review before any sale.

objections.question: Can customers be reached?
objections.objection: Carpenters are price sensitive and the buyer (homeowner) rarely chooses fittings. A ₹2,499 add-on per wardrobe is untested.

critique:cpt_a38a414885.strongest_point: It works whatever board was used and needs no chemistry or registration.
critique:cpt_a38a414885.simpler_alternative: Use adjustable cabinet legs already sold for modular kitchens to keep units off the floor, and publish a fitting guide that leaves an inspection gap. No new product is needed to test whether anyone cares.

objections.question: Does the business work financially?
objections.objection: The founder earns about ₹168 an hour against a ₹600 opportunity cost, and capacity caps at about 30 visits a month. It is a job, not a business, at this price.

objections.question: Does something similar already exist?
objections.objection: Third-party home inspection agencies already operate and charge by area, so the visit itself is not new.

objections.question: What could make this fail?
objections.objection: Boards can be swapped after the inspector leaves, and a visual check cannot confirm chemical treatment, so the report proves less than it seems.

objections.question: Is there a much simpler or more effective approach?
objections.objection: Much of the check (licence lookup) is free in the government's BIS Care app; the paid value must come from something the homeowner cannot do alone.

critique:cpt_53d7f7d4b8.strongest_point: Lowest capital (about ₹39,000 peak) and first revenue in about 24 days, so demand can be tested cheaply.
critique:cpt_53d7f7d4b8.simpler_alternative: Test willingness to pay with a ₹499 30-minute video verification call where the carpenter shows the boards, before any site visits.
